title: Bodhisattva Methods, Part 1: Giving continued
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett continues Nomon's series on Dogen's four bodhisattva methods with the second half of the section on giving, opening with Naomi Shihab Nye's poem "Shoulders." Nomon reads Dogen's stories of Emperor Tai of the Tang dynasty giving his beard as medicine and of a child offering sand to the Buddha and becoming King Ashoka, then tells of Ashoka's turn from conquest to Buddhism. Andy Goldsworthy's impermanent leaf chains and his ten-foot snowball left on a London sidewalk show giving as delight and surprise. Nomon asks what it would be to walk into work as an act of giving, and the discussion that follows closes on a participant's "Thanks mom" for a gift of curiosity about what lies down the trail.

sentences.text: Poem by Naomi Shihab Nye, called Shoulders.
A man crosses the street in rain, stepping gently, looking two times north and south, because his son is on his shoulder.
No car must splash him.
No car must drive too near his shadow.
This man carries the world's most sensitive cargo, but he's not marked.
Nowhere does his jacket say fragile handle with care.
His ear fills up with breathing.
He hears the hum.
He hears the hum of a boy's dream deep inside him.
We're not going to be able to live in this world if we're not willing to do what he's doing with one another.
The road will only be wide and the rain will never stop falling.
A man crosses the street in rain, stepping gently, looking two times north and south, because his son is asleep on his shoulder.
No car must splash him.
No car must drive.
He may drive too near to his shadow.
This man carries the world's most sensitive cargo, but he's not marked.
Nowhere does his jacket say fragile handle with care.
His ear fills up with breathing.
He hears the hum of a boy's dream deep inside.
We're not going to be able to live in this world if we're not willing to do what he's doing with one another.
The road will only be wide.
The rain will never stop falling.
Actually, I can't read that poem without cracking up, so that's pretty good.
So continuing with Dogen's advice to us how to live as bodhisattvas, he has four suggestions.
I don't know if this sounds familiar or not.
The first is that we practice giving.
Secondly, he suggests we practice kind speech.
Thirdly, we practice beneficial action.
And fourth, what he calls identity action, which hopefully we'll get to.
So I want to continue with this section on giving.
Remember talking about this, about giving kindness and non-greed?
The Buddha said, *this is Dogen, when a person who practices giving goes to an assembly, people take notice.
Know that the mind of such a person communicates subtly with others.
This being so, giving even a phrase or a verse of the truth, it will be a wholesome seed for this and other lifetimes.
Give your valuables even a penny, even a blade of grass.
It will be a wholesome root for this and other lifetimes.
The truth can turn into valuables.
Valuables can turn into the truth.
This is all because the giver is willing.* That's the last paragraph we read last time.
So some of these teachers hundreds of years ago, thousands of years ago, anticipated so many things.
But now we're doing advanced science to try to figure out mirror neurons and body language, altruism and the evolutionary basis of all this.
But this is true.
You think that when a person who practices giving goes to an assembly, when they enter the room, people notice.
You're like, wow, what a nice person.
And that there's a subtle communication.
There's a subtle communication.
And I think we get a little hung up on, since we're materialists, essentially, we get a little hung up on the value of the gift.
We've got to give a good gift.
It would be trivial to give somebody a crummy gift or a too small grift or an inappropriate gift.
We're bound by complex and little understood or discussed set of social norms about giving in different cultures, a little different versions.
In Japan, they're big on giving.
I remember one time in Japan, we went into a sandwich shop, like a 7-Eleven kind of sandwich shop.
And there just didn't happen to be any other customers in there.
There were two or three of us, clumsy Americans.
We went in and they were so excited, seemingly.
I don't know if they were just being...
We would say, oh, they're just being nice, but it's a different cultural norm.
So they were seemingly very excited to sell us whatever it was, a sandwich or something.
And then when we turned to leave, there were three or four of them.
They all came out from behind the counter to bow and thank us for coming into their shop.
So I think the way we think about it, the customers, like giving money, it's an exchange.
Maybe there's not any giving going on at all in our version.
It's just like capitalism, no gifts involved, just value, a value proposition.
But this really felt like we...
They felt so overjoyed that we gave them the gift of our presents in their little sandwich shop.
So they gave us a beautiful greeting when we left.
So it can be a greeting, a sandwich, a blade of grass, a penny.
And it's the giving itself, he's saying, that's powerful.
And the giving itself is transformational.
So you may think it's just a blade of grass, but it becomes a treasure, it becomes valuable.
You may think it's just a sumptuous thing you're giving, and it becomes the truth, if it's given with this spirit.
He goes on, and now he's going to tell us a few stories.
A king, and the translators have figured out that this is Emperor Tai of the Tang dynasty, but this king gave his beard as medicine to cure his retainer's disease.
And I've not so far been able to figure out what the story is there.
It's a giving of your body.
And he says, a child offered sand to Buddha and became King Ashoka in a later birth.
So he gave the Buddha sand.
They were not greedy for reward, but only shared what they could.
Share a beard, share a grain of sand.
To launch a boat or build a bridge is an act of giving.
If you study giving closely, you see that to accept a body and to give up the body are both giving.
This is a really interesting statement, powerful statement.
If we really study giving, we'll see that to accept a body and to give up the body are both giving, which is not usually how we think about the body.
We're tired of the body, it's aching, it's getting stiffer and fatter, and so on.
We don't see this accepting of a body as an act of giving.
So that would be interesting to explore for ourselves, each of us.
How is it an act of giving to receive this body?
And how is it an act of giving to give up the body, to give up the body?
And if you've ever spent time with people right at the moment of death, maybe you have some sense of that.
That it can be a great gift to give up the body.

Making a living and producing things can be nothing other than giving.
So we don't really think that way either, do we?
Making a living is just another exchange, like in the sandwich shop.

I'm giving you labor, you're supposed to give me money, and I'm very wound up about the exact value proposition and the particulars of that, and what kind of skills they have, and what kind of company or institution this is,

Wouldn't that be great?
Maybe we should save our pennies and pick a date in the future somewhere and go to India and see where the Buddha was born and enlightened and see some of these columns of King Ashoka,
because quite a few still exist.
Anyway, he ended up being a really great guy, the history suggests.
I was reading about him in the great source of all knowledge, Wikipedia.
In Wikipedia, they quote H.G.
Wells, who wrote an enormous world history.
I'd have forgotten that if I ever knew it.
H.G.
Wells, in addition to all the fiction and radio plays

He wrote a big book of world history.

Anyway, they quote H.G.

Wells talking about King Ashoka, in North Asia, and Wells wrote, *Amidst the tens of thousands of names of monarchs that crowd the columns of history, their majesties and graciousnesses and serenities and royal highnesses and all the like, the name Ashoka shines and shines, almost alone as a star.*
So anyway, King Ashoka was...
So he tried to create a...

So there's another research project.

We're starting to change our mind.
We're starting to rewire our brain.

Keep on.
Keep on changing the minds through giving of sentient beings from the moment that you offer one valuable to the moment that they attain the way.
